name: Monolith, Modular Monolith and Microservices
intent: Choose how many separately deployed units a system is cut into, by counting what each cut costs: deploys and teams per change, network calls per request, and what fails together.
scenario: A shop has six modules: catalog, cart, orders, payments, shipping and notifications, with one team per module. The first version is one deployable with one database, and every release needs all six teams. The company splits it into six services, and a checkout now makes 5 network calls. A second attempt shares one database and a common library between the services, and a column rename still needs all six teams to deploy together. A third attempt cuts each module into three services, and one checkout makes 17 calls.
problem: "Monolith or microservices" sounds like a choice between old and new, but it is really two separate questions: where the module boundaries are, and where the deployment boundaries are. A monolith with no internal boundaries makes every change a negotiation between teams. Microservices move the boundaries onto the network, which buys independent deploys and isolated failures, and charges for them with network calls, partial failure, versioned contracts and an operations load. The bad result is the distributed monolith: services that still share a database and release together, so it pays the network cost and keeps the coupling. A modular monolith, with strict module boundaries inside one deployable, is the middle choice that many teams find enough. Practitioners disagree on where the line is, and the answer depends on team count and how often modules change independently.

howItWorks.title: Draw module boundaries first
howItWorks.text: A module owns a business capability and its data, and others reach it only through a published interface. This is the same work in every option: if the boundaries are wrong, cutting along them into services only makes the mistake expensive to fix. A big ball of mud has no such boundary, so callers reach into internals and a change to one module spreads to its callers.

howItWorks.title: Choose the deployment boundary separately
howItWorks.text: A deployable is a unit that is built, released and rolled back as one. In a monolith and a modular monolith all modules are in one deployable, so every team's change goes out in the same release. In microservices each module (or small group of modules) is its own deployable, so a team can release alone, if the contract it exposes does not change.

howItWorks.title: Count the network calls the cut adds
howItWorks.text: Inside one process a call between modules costs almost nothing and cannot partially fail. Across services every call adds latency, can time out and needs a retry or fallback decision. Count the calls in your most common request: a request that crosses 5 service boundaries pays for 5 round trips and has 5 places to fail.

howItWorks.title: Give each service its own data
howItWorks.text: Independent deploys only work if the service owns its tables and nobody else reads them. If two services share a database, a column rename or a long lock affects both, and they have to release together. A shared library can have the same effect: when a change to it must reach every service at once (a shared data model, say), every service that uses it has to rebuild and redeploy together.

howItWorks.title: Check blast radius and team cost together
howItWorks.text: Services contain a crash to one unit only if callers have timeouts and fallbacks. Without them, a failure in payments takes down the callers waiting on it. In one process a crash or a memory leak in any module takes down all modules. Pick the cut that matches the number of teams and the changes you really see, and be ready to move it.

pros: A monolith is the simplest to build, test, run and debug, with in-process calls and one transaction
A modular monolith keeps that simplicity and adds enforced boundaries, so modules can be split later
Microservices let a team release, scale and roll back its own unit without asking the others
A service crash or slow query can be contained to that service when callers have timeouts and fallbacks
cons: Every deployable shares one release train in a monolith, so team count raises waiting and merge conflicts
Services add network latency, partial failure, versioned contracts, and tracing and operations work
A shared database or shared library turns services into a distributed monolith that pays both costs
One process means one crash, one memory leak or one bad deploy affects all modules
whenToUse: Start with a monolith, or a modular monolith, when the team is small and the domain is still being learned
Split a module into a service when it needs its own release pace, its own scaling, or a failure boundary
Use services when many teams change different parts at the same time and the release train has become the bottleneck
whenNotToUse: Splitting into services before the module boundaries are known, because moving a boundary between services is far harder than between modules
Splitting for fashion or hiring reasons when one team owns the whole system
Splitting while keeping one shared database, since the services will still deploy together
pitfalls: The distributed monolith: separate services that share a database or a library and must be released in lockstep, so they pay for the network without the independence
Nanoservices: cutting each module into several tiny services, so one request makes 17 calls instead of 5
Treating microservices as a goal, rather than a way to get independent deploys for teams that need them
Calling a monolith bad when its real problem is missing module boundaries, which a modular monolith fixes without a network
Ignoring that a monolith shares fate: one memory leak in any module takes every module down
No timeouts or fallbacks between services, so a failure in payments still takes down every caller waiting on it
Counting only how easy a new service is to start, and not the cost of running, tracing and upgrading many of them

quiz.question: A shop splits into six services, but all of them read one shared database and use one shared library. Renaming a column in the orders table now requires all six services to be edited and deployed. What is this?
options: A healthy microservice design, because each service has its own repository.
A distributed monolith: it pays for network calls and keeps the coupling of one codebase.
A modular monolith, because the modules are still separate.
A nanoservice design, because the services are small.
quiz.explanation: Independent deploys depend on each service owning its data and contract. With a shared database and library, a change still spreads to every service and they release together, while every call now also crosses the network.

quiz.question: A team of eight wants clear boundaries and simple operations, but not network calls between its modules. Which option fits best?
options: Microservices, because boundaries need a network to be real.
A big ball monolith, because boundaries cost too much.
Nanoservices, so each module is as small as possible.
A modular monolith: one deployable, with module boundaries enforced inside it.
quiz.explanation: Boundaries are enforced by who may call what and who owns which data, and that can be checked in code inside one process. The team keeps in-process calls and one deploy, and can split a module out later if it needs its own release or scaling.

quiz.question: A bug in Payments leaks memory until its process runs out of memory and dies. In a well-built microservice design with timeouts and fallbacks, how many modules stop working, compared with a modular monolith?
options: All six in both, since the shop is one system.
Only payments in the microservice design, but every module in the monolith, because all modules share the process that dies.
None in either, because crashes are always contained.
Only payments in both, because modules are isolated by their interfaces.
quiz.explanation: A crash or a memory leak in a monolith takes down the whole process. Separate services contain it to one unit, if callers use timeouts and fallbacks. Module interfaces isolate code, not the failure of a shared process.
